context: a letter from W. E. Darwin, which you are answering
exchanges:
I enclose what flowers I could find of the different kinds; I am afraid it is doubtful whether you will find any pollen, as the flowers are very much past. I suppose it will turn out all rubbish, & I think gradations will probably turn up.

Still I think it ought to be the explanation, as it is much neater— And I do not quite see how supposing it to have been originally hermaphrodite & female explains it, as tho’ one can understand hermaphrodite become male, why should the female become male?

I enclose outlines of pollen, & styles cut off close to ovary.

There is a great difference in the length of papillæ on the two male flower stigmas; the long styled is much the roughest

I hope the twigs will grow; one has taken root in my friend Dunn’s garden.

I am going to look at the white broom this evening.

I am glad the boys are going a trip in Wales.

I hope mamma is pretty brisk

The cuttings arrived in good time & were at once planted, & this morning your grand collection of sketches arrived: many thanks for all your great trouble— Your drawings show considerable difference in the two pollens, & I now believe in your discovery, which seems to me, a very curious one.—

The anthers received this morning contained pollen too shrivelled to measure.— Next summer I must get you to send me some fresh flowers, & you must look a little more for gradation in form.— It will not do for you to publish, I think, till we have tested power of the two pollens on the two females.— It is just possible size of grains may vary in different trees.— The whole case seems to me eminently well worth working out.—

I have to pay Elinor Carter £2"16"8 for your expences at Paris.— You must let me hear sometime how balance is between your journey & Etty’s napoleons—

your affect Father | C. Darwin

I suppose stamens do not differ in length in the two males
